title: Nepal’s flood claim tests whether a nascent climate fund can deliver - Mongabay India
description: Nepal’s flood claim tests whether a nascent climate fund can deliver  Mongabay India
publisher.title: Mongabay India
full_article:
Nepal has approached the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage for quick relief following the August 26 floods.

Himalayan warming is accelerating, but experts say this specific flood can’t yet be conclusively linked to climate change alone.

The global climate fund’s resources are insufficient to meet global demand as well as Nepal’s losses, and it’s unclear if the fund can respond quickly enough when there is a crisis. See All Key Ideas

More than 1,386 people have died and over 5,130 more missing, as of September 12, following the August 26 floods in Nepal. In the wreckage along the Bhote Koshi river lie two unresolved questions: Is climate change linked to the disaster? And, can a nascent global fund, built to help vulnerable countries in such crises, actually deliver?

Soon after the floods, the Government of Nepal wrote a letter to the Board of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), a financial mechanism of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) established in 2022 to help vulnerable countries cope with climate disasters.

In the letter signed by the country’s Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle and Minister for Agriculture, Forest and Environment Gita Chaudhary, Nepal requested the board to take a special decision to respond rapidly, directly and effectively. Signed on August 31, the letter emphasised that a prompt response would “demonstrate that the Fund can translate international solidarity into timely support for vulnerable countries and communities when it is most urgently needed.”

Nepal contributes roughly 0.027% of global greenhouse gas emissions. The mountainous country is in the ‘least developed country’ category designated by the UN and is a highly climate-vulnerable country that “continues to bear disproportionate and escalating climate impacts,” the letter states. It argues that the Bhote Koshi disaster demonstrates how extreme events in the cryosphere can rapidly cascade and compound from high mountains to densely populated downstream areas, affecting water, food, energy, health, infrastructure and ecosystems.

Though the letter puts no figure on it, Nepal’s direct damage from this single event is estimated at $2.6 billion, according to Sravan Shrestha, a remote sensing and geoinformation specialist with the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD)’s Cryosphere and Water Risks programme. Reconstruction and recovery could cost $4-5 billion or more, he says.

Buildings destroyed after flash floods in August at the confluence of Trishuli and Tadi rivers in Devighat, Nuwakot district in Nepal. (AP Photo/Rajesh Kumar Singh)

The attribution tension

On the morning of August 26, a bedrock slope underneath a hanging glacier failed at roughly 5,200 metres on the north face of the Langtang Himal. The mass fell about 1,200 metres from the avalanche source, leading to a rock-ice avalanche, and then headed towards the Lhende Khola at about 2,900 metres, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi. Friction from the fall melted ice and generated enough water to turn the avalanche into a debris flow, releasing a hyper-concentrated surge downstream into already swollen rivers, according to the ICIMOD assessment.

Within a few hours, it had turned into the disaster that killed more than a thousand people, with many families still awaiting news of their loved ones. However, it is still unclear whether this crisis was a result of climate change, and how will this shape FRLD’s decision to aid Nepal.

“Not all of the devastating impacts of the Nepal-Tibet floods are due to climate change,” cautions Emily Wilkinson, a Principal Research Fellow in ODI’s Global Risks and Resilience Programme. Warming temperatures likely worsened the flooding’s extent, but how badly households were hit also came down to uneven development, weak investment in disaster risk reduction, social marginalisation in some cases, and geopolitical factors, she says. Attributable loss and damage can be calculated once a climate attribution study is available, adds Wilkinson, who works with a UK-based think tank.

Shrestha, from ICIMOD, says, climate change may be one of the major factors, but confirming that requires further investigation. What isn’t in doubt, is the broader trend: the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) is warming at roughly twice the global average at 0.3°C per decade, with glacier mass projected to shrink dramatically by 2100. A comprehensive 2026 glacier assessment, based on 30 years of Landsat data, shows the region has lost 12% of its glacier area since 1990, with the rate of loss 50% higher in the last decade than in the 1990s. As glaciers retreat, they progressively remove the support once holding the bedrock beneath them in place, he says.

“However, whether it caused that particular slope to collapse on that particular morning is a question nobody has answered, and it is early to claim otherwise,” he says.

“In the 2000s, we expected a glacial-origin flood in the HKH roughly once every 5 to 10 years. In 2025 alone, three such events hit the region, and now this in 2026,” he adds.

Raju Pandit Chhetri, Executive Director of Kathmandu-based non-profit Prakriti Resource Centre, points to three lines of evidence: global warming trends already predict disasters of exactly this kind; the Himalayas are warming faster than the global average due to their fragile mountain ecology; and Nepal itself has seen such events recur systematically, including a glacial lake outburst flood in the Everest region just two years ago. “If they say these are not the kind of events that climate change is going to bring, then those questioning it, whether the FRLD or other developed countries, are just shying away from their own responsibility. They should prove the incident was not because of climate change,” he says.

Experts point to a lack of preparedness that also played a role in worsening heavy damage. Shrestha underlines the biggest gap related to early warning systems. He says that the hazard came from a source nobody was watching. Nepal has a well-developed inventory of 47 potentially dangerous glacial lakes, and early warning systems exist at two of them: Tsho Rolpa and Imja Tsho.

Imja Tsho lake and glacier. Nepal has a well-developed inventory of 47 potentially dangerous glacial lakes, and early warning systems exist at only two of them: Tsho Rolpa and Imja Tsho. Image by Daniel Alton Byers via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0).

But the August 26 event did not start from a lake, he says. It started from a bedrock slope with a hanging glacier, a source no regional inventory tracks. The monitoring stations that did exist were also too fragile and slow, he adds. Automated river gauges at Bhote Koshi and Syabrubesi were meant to detect rising water and trigger alerts. Instead, the flood swept them away before any warning could be issued. The flood reached Syabrubesi within roughly ten minutes of crossing into Nepal.

The early warning systems that do exist, in any case, are calibrated for gradual monsoon flooding, not a hyper concentrated debris flow in minutes, he says.

The capacity question

The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) is an idea that took decades to become reality. Small island nations had pushed for a loss and damage mechanism since at least 1991, during negotiations that led to the UN climate convention which was formally established in 1992. In 2015, Article 8 of the Paris Agreement formally addressed loss and damage as a distinct pillar of climate action. Finally, at COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh in 2022, countries agreed to establish the fund.

The fund was operationalised the following year at COP28 in Dubai, where the summit’s presidency, the United Arab Emirates, pledged $100 million and called on other nations to contribute. Pledges to the fund now exceed $820 million.

As of the fund’s most recent board meeting in July, 119 countries had submitted 176 funding requests of approximately $2.8 billion. The response was significant enough that the board decided it needed additional time for a comprehensive, rigorous assessment of the full portfolio before approving anything. It pushed the decision to its next meeting, scheduled for December 2026 in Manila.

“Even though the FRLD is still in the process of finalising its operational and design features, one thing is already clear: the resources currently available are orders of magnitude below the scale of actual loss and damage needs,” said Vera Künzel, Senior Advisor for Climate Change Adaptation and Human Rights at Germanwatch, a German non-profit known for publishing the Global Climate Risk Index, an annual ranking of countries most affected by extreme weather events.

The fund was welcomed with great enthusiasm and high expectations, but it is currently far from being able to meet those expectations, she adds.

Nepal’s request adds a further complication. It is not a standard proposal seeking project-based support, but an appeal for immediate, rapid response. Rapid response is a distinctive feature of FRLD’s design, setting it apart from other climate finance mechanisms. However, it has not yet built the machinery to deliver.

Nepal’s direct damage from this single event is estimated at $2.6 billion, according to an expert from ICIMOD. Reconstruction and recovery could cost $4-5 billion or more. Representative image by Lawrence Hislop/GRID-Arendal via Flickr (CC BY-NC-SA 2.0).

Wilkinson and Chhetri echo the same. “The fund’s governing instrument explicitly allows it to support rapid response measures. However, under the Barbados Implementation Modalities (BIM), the name given to its pilot phase, there is no provision to do so,” says Wilkinson. “Applications to the fund currently being reviewed far outstrip funds available, and so it would have to reject some of these in order to provide funding to Nepal. There are other humanitarian funds and organisations better positioned to provide rapid response funding — like the UN’s Central Emergency Response Fund.”

Chhetri says that FRLD has the provision of rapid response in its governing instrument, though the modalities are not yet fleshed out on how to operationalise that part of its governing instrument. “For now, the Board can agree to support Nepal as a case of urgency, while working out the modalities later,” he says.

At a recent Least Developed Countries (LDC) Group ministerial meeting in Dili, Timor-Leste on September 3, member states expressed solidarity with the people of Nepal. They adopted a declaration flagging that demand for FRLD support already far exceeds the fund’s available resources, and calling for clearer guidance on mobilising additional funding.

Nepal’s request, is strongly backed by other LDCs and developing nations, Künzel says. She expects the board to respond positively. The “polluter pays” principle is well established in international environmental and climate policy and reflected in the broader architecture of the Paris Agreement. Support for countries like Nepal is not charity but an obligation rooted in responsibility and fairness, she says.

Beyond that, it tests whether the multilateral system can be trusted to function when it is needed most, she says.

title: More than 5,000 people remain missing after floods in Nepal - UA.NEWS
description: More than 5,000 people remain missing after floods in Nepal  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, in the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli river corridor near the border with China, more than 5,130 people are considered missing after sudden floods. Nearly three weeks after the disaster, authorities are shifting from search-and-rescue operations to providing aid and reconstruction, Deutsche Welle English reports.

At least 1,386 bodies have been found in five affected districts. Those missing include 587 foreigners and around 900 workers in hydropower tunnels and other energy facilities. According to authorities, the floods were caused by a glacier collapse. The water destroyed communities and swept away more than a dozen hydropower facilities.

Destroyed villages and isolated communities

In the upper reaches of the rivers, entire settlements disappeared within minutes. Destroyed roads and bridges have complicated access to some areas, so rescuers and humanitarian services are delivering essential supplies by helicopter. Searches continue in flooded tunnels and along silt-covered banks.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

In Uttargaya, in Rasuwa district, at least 618 houses were washed away or buried, and 877 people have still not been found. Only 12 bodies have been recovered there. Chameli Gurung, deputy head of the local municipality, said that public land in the area has either been washed away or become unsafe, forcing relatives of the dead to travel to the Pashupati Aryaghat cremation complex in Kathmandu. Local authorities are considering renting private land to accommodate displaced families until winter.

Reconstruction will cost billions

According to local media reports, a preliminary rapid assessment of damage and recovery needs put reconstruction needs at approximately 723.3 billion Nepalese rupees — about $4.78 billion. According to the RDNA assessment, nearly two-thirds of this amount may be needed to restore energy and transport networks, as well as educational institutions.

Hydropower provides almost all of Nepal's electricity and has become an important source of the country's export revenue. According to Reuters, India approved electricity exports to Nepal for 18 hours a day at least until December 31. Nepal has also sought assistance from the Loss and Damage Fund supported by the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and says it intends to build infrastructure more resilient to climate risks.

title: Climate catastrophe leaves Nepal mourning while the search for the missing continues - Focus - France 24
description: Climate catastrophe leaves Nepal mourning while the search for the missing continues - Focus  France 24
publisher.title: France 24
full_article:
Authorities now face the daunting task of recovering and identifying hundreds of bodies, many of them severely damaged by the floodwaters. Meanwhile, families of those still missing remain in agonising uncertainty as rescue operations continue.

For survivors, the conditions are equally harsh. Thousands of homes have been destroyed or rendered uninhabitable. Water sources have been contaminated, while essential infrastructure has been badly damaged. They now face the long aftermath: finding shelter, accessing medical care, burying their dead and eventually, rebuilding their lives.

Faced with the scale of the destruction, Nepalese authorities are increasingly turning to the issue of climate justice. Nepal contributes only a tiny share of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet it is among the countries bearing the brunt of climate change. Kathmandu now wants to change its message on the international stage. Rather than simply calling for emergency aid, it is demanding compensation for the losses and damage caused by climate change.

title: Nepal’s Water Infrastructure Is Failing, So Residents Are Reviving an Ancient Solution - Next City
description: Nepal’s Water Infrastructure Is Failing, So Residents Are Reviving an Ancient Solution  Next City

full_article:
Story by Pratik Ghimire Published on Sep 14, 2026

Before the streets of Nepal’s Bramhakhel fill with traffic, 40-year-old Pratima Poudel walks to a centuries-old stone spout carrying empty plastic bottles to collect water. The walk has become part of the Nepali language instructor’s daily routine.

The spout she visits each morning is part of the Kathmandu Valley’s traditional water system, composed of interconnected stone spouts known locally as dhunge dhara or alternately as hiti. The network once supplied water to communities across the valley; today, it provides an alternative source for residents facing unreliable access to piped water.

“We don’t like tap water,” she tells Next City as she fills her bottles directly from the spout. From time to time, residents treat the spout’s water with chlorine. “This water is cleaner. Some neighbors have begun boiling the water before drinking, but I am not worried.”

In a country where only a quarter of the population has access to clean drinking water, Poudel is one of a growing number of Kathmandu residents choosing the spout over the tap. Nearly 70% of the city’s drinking water samples contain E. coli and faecal coliform, bacteria that indicate contamination by human or animal waste, according to the latest government analysis. Residents say the valley’s rivers have become open sewers and the pipes carry the same contamination into their homes.

Climate change and rapid urbanization are colliding in the Southeast Asian country, where increased monsoon intensity and frequent floods are overwhelming the capital’s water systems. Amid this failure of modern infrastructure, residents are reviving dhunge dharas in and around Kathmandu — in one case, even rebuilding an ancient fountain from the ground up after it was lost in the 2015 earthquake.

Pratima Poudel fills her water bottle at Brahmakhel Dhunge Dhara in Kathmandu, Nepal. (Photo by Pratik Ghimire)

A 1,400-year-old network

The oldest functioning spout — Manga Hiti in Patan, a city of ancient palaces and courtyards less than four miles south of central Kathmandu — has provided water since 570 AD.

These fountains rely on underground aquifers that channel water naturally through gravitational force, supported by networks of ponds and canals that store and regulate supply during dry seasons while preventing flooding during monsoons.

Beneath each stone spout lies a complex water system. A stone spout is essentially “the outlet of a spring connected to groundwater,” as climate change and springshed expert Ujjwal Upadhyay describes it.

“The stone structure is built by people, but the water flowing through it comes from a natural underground system,” he explains.

Rainwater enters the ground through a defined recharge area, accumulates in underground aquifers and eventually emerges at the surface as a spring. Traditionally, communities identified these natural water pathways and built spouts at points where water could flow to the surface.

“Even those who get tap water come to Bhinya Hiti for drinking water,” says heritage conservationist Rabindra Puri, referring to a spout in Bhaktapur municipality, about eight miles from Kathmandu. It’s believed to date back around 1,400 years.

“The spouts served a social purpose as well as providing water,” he explains. “They were designed as community spaces where residents could meet, exchange news, and socialize while collecting water, much like people gathering at tea shops today.”

The Bhinya Hiti fountain in Bhaktapur, an ancient city in Nepal's Kathmandu Valley. (Photo by Pratik Ghimire

Short supply, uncertain quality

The public utility company Kathmandu Upatyaka Khanepani Limited is responsible for the management of the Kathmandu Valley’s water supply and sanitation system. Its 2024-2025 annual report says the capital’s water demand is about 136 million gallons (514 million liters) per day, while the company’s average supply is only 61.4 million (232.4 million liters) daily with seasonal variation.

The gap between supply and demand has pushed people to alternatives like groundwater extraction, private tankers, jars, and bottled water. But in places where functioning stone spouts are available, people continue to use dhunge dharas.

For 18-year-old Mohin Thapa, Brahmakhel Dhunge Dhara has made collecting drinking water easier.

“When my parents are busy with work, I collect the water myself,” the university student says. “Rather than going every day, I fill four or five bottles at a time, which lasts a couple of days.”

His family uses tap water for bathing, cleaning, gardening and washing, while relying on water from the stone spout for drinking.

“I prefer drinking water from the dhunge dhara,” he tells Next City . “Ever since I was a child, that has been my primary water source, and I love its natural taste and freshness.”

Children drink water from Alko Hiti in the city of Patan. (Photo by Pratik Ghimire)

Sher Bahadur Pun, chief of the Tropical and Infectious Disease Hospital’s Clinical Research Unit, says the hospital receives around half a dozen patients presenting with symptoms of waterborne diseases, including fever and diarrhea, every day. Patients do not typically identify stone-spout water as the source of their illness, he says, but he still encourages caution.

“That does not make untreated stone-spout water automatically safe,” Pun says. “Boiling or purifying would be better.”

A 2022 review of research on Kathmandu Valley’s stone spouts reported that previous testing had detected total coliforms, E. coli and nitrates in some spout-water samples, with water quality varying by season. The review noted that many stone spouts rely on shallow groundwater, making them vulnerable to contamination.

A system under pressure

A survey by the Kathmandu Valley Water Supply Management Board in 2019 counted 573 spouts in the valley with a combined discharge of 2.4 million liters a day.

Of those spouts, many were in disrepair and 94 had been lost entirely. Just 224 were still functioning. In 2022, the valley’s water fountains were placed on the the World Monuments Fund’s watchlist for heritage sites urgently at risk.

Like the city’s modern water infrastructure, the ancient water network has also been increasingly under pressure due to extreme weather and development. Kathmandu receives around 57 inches (1,450 millimetres) of rainfall a year, but more often, that rain is falling in shorter, more intense periods, Upadhyay says.

“Heavy rainfall over a short duration is more likely to run off rather than infiltrate and recharge groundwater,” Upadhyay points out.

Houses, roads, agriculture and other changes in land use can interfere with the areas where water needs to infiltrate, he explains: “A spout can be cleaned, repaired or restored on the surface, but if its underground conduits are broken, its recharge area is blocked, or its water source has been disrupted, the flow can disappear.”

Sushil Shrestha stands beside Alko Hiti in the city of Patan, Nepal. (Photo by Pratik Ghimire)

Sushil Shrestha, a stone-spout expert, conservationist and chairperson of the Historic Stone Spouts and Ponds Conservation Association, says that this has happened at stone spouts across the valley.

He points to Sundhara, or the Golden Spout, in Kathmandu, where surrounding buildings and infrastructure have disrupted the underground system and contributed to the spout drying up. But he says the spout could still be revived by reconnecting it to viable water sources.

Bringing spouts back to life

Residents are now more aware of the importance of this heritage, Shrestha says.

The nearly 600- to 700-year-old Alko Hiti in Patan, Lalitpur — which alone produces more than 200,000 gallons (about 800,000 liters) of water a day, he says — was restored after its water was polluted from a leak from a local bone mill factory in 2000. A surge in water-borne diseases triggered a local conservation movement, which culminated in the community-led revival and renovation of Alko Hiti in 2003.

In Thamel, the historic Ga Hiti spout supplied thousands of residents until April 2015, when a neighbouring hotel collapsed in a massive earthquake that devastated the region, and the spout was destroyed. Reconstruction cost more than $30,000 (Rs4.6 million), with Kathmandu Metropolitan City covering 80% and residents raising the rest. The Ga Hiti Youth Club and local volunteers finished the work in about six months, and the spout was flowing again by early 2017.

According to Shrestha, there is a massive gap between water demand and supply, and functioning dhunge dhara are “actively helping to minimize that gap.”

“They are priceless ancient heritage and very old living historic monuments – beyond easing daily shortages,” he tells Next City . “If Kathmandu Valley loses them or they stop flowing, the water crisis will deepen further, and we will lose a very important part of our history.”

The deluge, triggered by the collapse of a glacier, has killed nearly 1,400 people in Nepal and Tibet. Keystone-SDA

Nearly three weeks after devastating floods struck Nepal and Tibet, Swiss engineer Eric Bardou says conditions on the ground remain challenging and calls for a better understanding of such events to help prevent future disasters.

“You could say it almost feels like an earthquake,” said Eric Bardou, a member of the Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit (SHA), in a telephone call to the Keystone-ATS news agency from Kathmandu on Saturday. On the ground he saw buildings destroyed or displaced by the force of the wave, some of which appeared to have been pushed sideways.

The 57-year-old engineer, who specialises in geotechnical engineering, hydrology and mountain risks, was sent to Nepal by Switzerland on September 5. He was integrated into the mission of the United Nations Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), where his role involved assessing risks related to water and terrain.

On his arrival, two lakes that had formed as a result of landslides raised fears of a new wave. “They drained on their own, but it is the sort of situation that still needed to be monitored,” he explained. The teams had to set up observation points and adjust their movements to ensure they were not caught off guard by a new rise in water levels.

Preserving evidence

The Swiss expert, who is soon returning from Nepal, highlights another, less visible urgency: preserving the traces of the disaster before they disappear.

“If we don’t do it now, we will never be able to understand what happened,” he stresses. But behind these traces lies, above all, a human tragedy.

Bardou said he was deeply moved seeing people wandering along the riverbanks, searching for missing relatives or for items that might be salvaged from the rubble. International organisations on the ground are meanwhile focused on trying to rescue those still alive beneath the rubble.

More

The hope to be able to document the disaster, however, is confronted with a fundamental difficulty: estimates vary widely depending on the methods used, particularly concerning the volume of collapsed material.

“The volume swept downstream is estimated at between 100 and almost 300 million cubic metres,” Bardou explains. He claims to have seen various estimates and is unable to determine which is the most reliable, especially as he has been unable to access the area where the deluge began.

On August 26, rock and ice broke away at an altitude of approximately 5,200 metres on the north face of the Langtang Lirung massif. Debris quickly descended downstream along the Lhende Khola river valley, situated some 20 kilometres upstream of the Gyirong/Rasuwagadhi border pass, completely obliterating the Sino-Nepalese border at that point. The deluge killed nearly 1,400 people in Nepal and Tibet.

More

Read more: Himalayan flood sparks concern among Nepalese and Tibetans in Switzerland

Another unknown factor is the exact composition of the mass that poured down the valley. The traces observed downstream indicate a particularly fluid flow containing vast volumes of water and boulders, some of which were several metres in diameter.

‘Fluid’ torrential debris flow

By comparing marks left on trees and buildings with the deposits on the ground, Bardou estimates that 80% of the mass consisted of water.

The disaster has also left behind a considerable amount of sediment and caused heavy erosion. Some bodies have been found downstream as far as India, at a distance of between 150 and 240 kilometres, demonstrating the enormous power.

Bardou says the challenge is to better understand the mechanisms behind this disaster rather than settling for a simple explanation linked to climate change. “To say that it’s hot, that the ice is melting and that everything is collapsing is a bit too simplistic,” he said.

More

But the link with global warming is less obvious for large natural disasters. Read more: Why do Swiss mountains collapse? It’s complicated

Climate change can cause rapid transformations to which the mountains must adapt, he said. Permafrost, which acts like a cement holding certain rocks and soil together, may play a special role. But he says he’s not totally satisfied with this as the sole explanation. Society needs to determine exactly what happened in order to identify and prevent such events, he adds.

Prevention is difficult

Prevention measures, however, are hampered by the sheer scale of the Himalayas: 600,000 km² compared with the 25,000 km² of the Swiss Alps. “The scale radically changes the situation,” he said.

In Switzerland, the large number of observers, guides, engineers and sensors makes it easier to detect mountain movements and changes.

In Nepal, institutions and specialists have been working on glaciers and mountain risks for some time. But even with satellite images showing a possible acceleration in an area prior to the event, you still needs to know where to look among the vast amounts of data, says the Valais native.

The glacier at the root of the disaster is now a central focus. Until then, the priority had been to rescue those who could still be saved.

title: Floods damage 1,843 tons of vegetables in Nepal - freshplaza.com
description: Floods damage 1,843 tons of vegetables in Nepal  freshplaza.com
publisher.title: freshplaza.com
full_article:
Flash floods that affected the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river system on August 26 caused losses to vegetable cultivation across several areas of Nepal, according to a Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment report prepared by the National Planning Commission and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

The assessment found that 137 hectares of vegetable crops were affected, resulting in an estimated loss of 1,843 tons of vegetables.

Bidur in Nuwakot recorded the largest impact, with 98 hectares of vegetable crops affected and an estimated potential loss of 1,323 tons.

Vegetable growing areas were also affected in Dhading. This included nine hectares in Benighat Rorang, seven hectares in Gajuri, two hectares in Siddhalek, and 14 hectares in Galchhi.

The assessment identified affected local levels across Nuwakot, Dhading, and Gorkha, including Bidur, Likhu, Belkotgadhi, Benighat Rorang, Gajuri, Siddhalek, Galchhi, Gandaki, and Shahid Lakhan.

title: India approves expedited export of electricity to flood-hit Nepal - The Hindu
description: India approves expedited export of electricity to flood-hit Nepal  The Hindu
publisher.title: The Hindu
full_article:
India’s Ministry of Power have given their go-ahead for exporting power to Nepal to help recover from devastating floods which, among other things, destroyed their hydropower infrastructure and took lives of more than 1,300 people.

The approval paves the way for exporting power for 18 hours a day starting Sept 13 until Dec 31 this year.

Nepal flash floods: What caused the devastation?

“The approval will help Nepal meet its power requirements during this difficult period and further strengthen the close and longstanding energy cooperation between India and Nepal,” stated India’s Power Ministry.

It further informed the quantum of power to be exported from January next year would be reviewed in December.

Nepal flash floods wash away illusions of clean, easy hydropower

The Hindu had earlier reported that Kathmandu had asked New Delhi to accord requisite approvals for transmission of electricity earlier than usual.

Nepal usually imports electricity from India during the winter months, starting around October, as power generation is typically low in the Himalayan country during the freezing winter months.

Conversely, the country exports its excess hydropower to India during the summer.

According to official data, India imported 3,299 million units (MUs) of power from Nepal in fiscal year 2025-26 and exported 1,451 MUs to it.

title: India approves 18-hour power supply as Nepal floods death toll crosses 1,300 - Firstpost
description: India approves 18-hour power supply as Nepal floods death toll crosses 1,300  Firstpost
publisher.title: Firstpost
full_article:
India has moved to provide faster electricity supplies to Nepal after devastating floods damaged hydropower infrastructure and left more than 1,300 people dead.

The Ministry of Power has approved an expedited export of electricity to the neighbouring country, allowing Kathmandu to meet its energy needs while recovery efforts continue.

Under the approval, Nepal will receive power for up to 18 hours a day from September 13 to December 31, 2026. The decision comes as the flood-hit country struggles with reduced domestic power generation following extensive damage to hydropower projects.

Nepal's death toll from the disaster has risen to 1,344, with rescue teams continuing to search for survivors and hundreds of children and others still reported missing in the worst-affected areas. The floods have also displaced thousands and damaged homes and other critical infrastructure.

Advertisement

India approves up to 654 MW supply

India has cleared the export of up to 600 MW through the Muzaffarpur-Dhalkebar 400 kV transmission line. Another 54 MW can be supplied through the Tanakpur-Mahendranagar 132 kV line.

The approved supply will run from midnight to 6 pm each day until the end of December. The Indian government said the arrangement would help Nepal deal with its immediate power shortage and further strengthen the two countries' long-standing energy cooperation.

The amount of electricity to be exported from January 2027 will be reviewed in December, according to the Ministry of Power.

More from World

The decision followed a request from Kathmandu for New Delhi to provide the necessary approval earlier than usual. Nepal normally increases its electricity imports from India during the winter months, when domestic generation falls because of lower water availability and colder conditions.

Flood damage deepens Nepal's power crisis

The floods have created an unusual situation for Nepal's power sector. The Himalayan nation generally produces surplus hydropower during the summer and exports electricity to India. During winter, however, it usually turns to Indian power supplies to meet the shortfall.

Official figures show that the energy relationship works in both directions. In fiscal year 2025-26, India imported 3,299 million units of electricity from Nepal, while exporting 1,451 million units to the country.

Advertisement

The recent disaster has disrupted that balance by damaging hydropower infrastructure and reducing Nepal's ability to generate electricity at home.

Disaster continues to take a heavy toll

The floods began on August 26 after a likely glacial collapse in the Himalayas triggered the formation of lakes. Huge quantities of water and debris then swept through valleys and settlements near Nepal's border with Tibet.

With the death toll now at 1,344, rescue and search operations remain underway. Thousands of survivors have been displaced, while authorities are also dealing with concerns over access to clean drinking water and the risk of disease in affected areas.

Power ministry said that the latest move reflected India's commitment to supporting Nepal during the crisis and strengthening bilateral cooperation in the energy sector.

title: A Flood Disaster in Nepal - Foreign Policy in Focus
description: A Flood Disaster in Nepal  Foreign Policy in Focus
publisher.title: Foreign Policy in Focus
full_article:
The flash floods that swept through Nepal on August 26 came from a glacial crash, 40 miles from Kathmandu, the country’s capital. A gigantic chunk of ice, half a kilometer thick, broke off a glacier and fell down a river with a seismic force of 5.2 magnitude. This mass of millions of tons of ice shattered on impact into a gushing stream that increased the level of the Bhote Koshi River, which sits at the intersection of the Sino-Nepali border, by nine meters. The Bhote Koshi River merges with the larger river system of Trishuli that, too, got bloated and pushed floodwater almost a hundred miles downstream across Nepal’s border into India.

As of September 5, as many as 1,350 people were listed dead and 5,000 missing. Initial estimates put the economic toll of the disaster at $5 billion, which is 10 percent of Nepal’s GDP. Kathmandu calls the disaster anything but natural and demands “justice and compensation” from “the world’s major emitters.”

Nepal is home to 3,808 Himalayan glaciers spanning 3,902 square kilometers with an ice cover of 286.1 billion cubic meters of water. These glaciers are, however, retreating fast. The reason behind their retreat is rapidly changing global climate. It is not just Nepal’s glaciers that are melting away. Nepal is part of the eight nations that share 54,000 Hindu Kush-Himalayas glaciers, which hold 5.6 trillion cubic meters of water. These glaciers, which are billed as the “water towers of Asia,” feed Asia’s 10 largest river systems. They are also known as the world’s “third pole,” the other two being the North and South Poles.

Although estimates vary, one-third of these glaciers will have melted away by the turn of the century, if global heating reaches 1.5 degree Celsius above preindustrial levels. This will be an irreparable loss for 2 billion people of the region, who depend upon them for drinking and irrigation supplies. A case in point is the Indus, which is one of the largest river systems in south Asia which depends on glaciers for 80 percent of its annual flow. The rapid melting of these glaciers, triggered by global heating, is the death knell for the region’s ecology, as well as its agriculture and agriculture-related industries.

Glaciers are fed by precipitation, especially the monsoons. As climate change has shortened the monsoon season, precipitation across the Hindu Kush-Himalayas has dropped in direct proportion. Worse still, global heating is thinning out the existing ice cover of the glaciers. Nepali glaciers have lost one-third of their ice cover. More importantly, the Himalayas are reportedly “warming twice as fast as the global average.” Although the glaciers at the top remain somewhat replenished by precipitation, climate change is stripping them bare at lower elevation.

The giant ice chunk that snapped off a glacier on August 26 was also at the lower elevation, where snowpack was too weak to hold it in place. In 2011-2020, the region’s glaciers melted 65 percent faster than the decade before. Climate change is, thus, hollowing out these glaciers in three ways. Lack of precipitation leaves them with ever-diminishing ice cover. Global heating is fast melting their preexisting ice cover. And the declining snow and ice cover, which is reflecting less and less sunlight, absorbs more and more heat, accelerating glacial melting in the process.

The site of the Nepali glacier that cracked up on August 26 was the Langtang Lirung peak close to the Langtang National Park, which borders Tibet in China. Around a hundred miles downstream, India also endured loss of life in the glacial collapse. As such it is a cross-national calamity. What gives it a global cast is the suspected loss of life of thousands of tourists from 34 countries, including 75 from the United States. These nations represent four continents of Africa, Americas, Asia, and Europe.

This is a snapshot of the global reach of fossil-fueled disasters that are increasing both in frequency and intensity by the year. Fossil fuels dug in Australia or burned in the United States have real life consequences half-way around the globe, to which even thousands of their own citizens are not immune. The global tale of woes, however, does not end here. On the Chinese side of the border, hundreds of tourists are unaccounted. Two weeks after the disaster, 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries are still missing in China. Although the Nepali government is trying hard to account for every tourist, hopes for their survival are dimming by the day.

The destructive force of the flooding can be gauged at the Sino-Nepali border crossing. Both sides of the border are crisscrossed with shiny customs and immigration buildings that, until before the disaster struck, stood tall. What happened to these buildings when the nine-meter high walls of water crashed into them is a harrowing sight to watch. It took only a second or two to rip them from their foundations and toss them like toys into torrents of water. The same held true for untold numbers of hapless staff and aspirant migrants who tried to sprint away only to be swallowed up by the tide in the blink of an eye.

The World Meteorological Organization confirms that the 11 years since 2015 were the hottest on record. Global temperatures have already reached 1.4 degree Celsius and are projected to reach 1.8 degree Celsius by midcentury, way over the maximum threshold of 1.5 degree Celsius agreed in the Paris Climate Pact.

Some attribute the recent accelerated warming to the El Nino effect, implying that all this global heating is transitory and fueled by a natural phenomenon. That’s not true. Even El Nino has grown 37 percent more intense due to global warming. El Nino is the result of warmer than normal waters in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean, a warming that is driven by climate change. Also, warming Pacific waters are supercharging El Nino. El Nino, in turn, is exacerbating the impact of climate change, making glacial collapses more frequent and even more fatal.

The flood disaster in Nepal is a canary in a coal mine. It should alert the world to the dangers of the continued use of fossil fuels and of not zeroing out emissions. The planet is warming, the glaciers are changing, and disasters just keep happening.

'Himalayan Flavor' has released the totals of their 'meal for Nepal' fundraiser.

title: NYC Restaurant Himalayan Yak Donates $5,000 from Buffet Sales to Nepal Flood Relief - nepyork
description: NYC Restaurant Himalayan Yak Donates $5,000 from Buffet Sales to Nepal Flood Relief  nepyork
publisher.title: nepyork
full_article:
JACKSON HEIGHTS, N.Y. — Himalayan Yak Restaurant has donated $5,000 to the Government of Nepal’s Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund to support flood relief efforts in Nepal after partnering with Nepal Run USA to raise money through buffet sales in Jackson Heights, organizers said.

The restaurant, located at 72-20 Roosevelt Ave., raised $4,070 through buffet purchases made by runners, customers and other community members. Himalayan Yak covered all food and preparation costs, allowing the full amount collected through buffet sales to go toward relief efforts.

The restaurant contributed an additional $930 from its own funds, bringing the total donation to $5,000.

Tsomo Dasel, owner of Himalayan Yak, said the contribution was intended to show solidarity with people affected by the flooding in Nepal.

“We could make this small contribution during this difficult time in Nepal,” Dasel said. “We just want to spread the message that we are with Nepal during this time.”

Founded in 2004, Himalayan Yak describes itself as New York City’s first Nepali restaurant. The Jackson Heights restaurant has become a longtime part of the neighborhood’s Himalayan food and cultural scene, serving dishes from Nepal, Tibet, Bhutan and India.

Its menu includes Nepali favorites such as momo, sekuwa, thali and wai wai sandeko, as well as Tibetan noodle dishes, Bhutanese specialties and Indian curries. The restaurant also features yak dishes and says it sources fresh yak meat from a farm during the summer.

Himalayan Yak is also known for its live music and full bar, making it a popular gathering place for community members and groups in Jackson Heights. The restaurant advertises live music seven nights a week, along with private dining and weekend buffet service.

The buffet sales brought together runners, restaurant patrons and members of the Nepali-American community in Jackson Heights, one of the centers of New York City’s Nepali and Himalayan diaspora.

The initiative was organized in partnership with Nepal Run USA as part of a broader community response to the flooding and related disasters in Nepal. Nepali-American organizations, businesses and individuals across the United States have been organizing relief efforts for affected communities.

The contribution comes as Nepali communities in New York and across the United States continue to mobilize financial support for people affected by the disaster.

title: Nepal adopts resolution on cooperation in nature conservation in Asia - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal adopts resolution on cooperation in nature conservation in Asia  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Kathmandu, Nepal, participants in the 6th Asian Congress for Conservation Biology adopted the Kathmandu Resolution 2026. It calls for stronger regional cooperation, leadership development and support for local and Indigenous communities in conserving biodiversity. This was stated in a commentary published by Mongabay.

The congress took place in early June under the theme “Harmonizing Biodiversity and Human Well-being in Asia.” It was organized by the Asian regional section of the Society for Conservation Biology together with the organization’s Nepal chapter and the Burhan Community Regeneration and Conservation Foundation.

Participants and program

Nearly 500 conservationists from 42 countries took part in the event. According to data cited in the commentary, 390 participants represented countries of the Global South, 357 were early-career professionals, and 151 were students. Another 38 people identified themselves as representatives of Indigenous or local communities, while 43% identified as women or members of gender minorities.

The program included 11 plenary speeches, 300 oral presentations across 24 sessions and 19 symposia, 59 poster presentations, as well as five afternoon and seven full-day workshops. Participants discussed the conservation of the Asiatic cheetah, Arabian and snow leopards, elephants, primates, birds, amphibians and reptiles, as well as human-wildlife interactions, the role of communities and conservation policy.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Content of the resolution

The Kathmandu Resolution calls for building the capacity of Asia’s conservation sector through peaceful regional interaction, the exchange of knowledge and experience, resource mobilization, and strengthening national chapters of the Society for Conservation Biology. The document also addresses the need to counter economic systems that view nature solely as capital for exploitation.

The resolution stresses the need to create conditions for leadership by students, women, gender minorities, Indigenous peoples and local communities. It calls for abandoning top-down conservation approaches in favor of models that recognize community rights, their independent decision-making, and the connection between nature conservation and public well-being.

The organizers provided nearly 160 participants with travel cost reimbursements, registration fee waivers or discounts. At the same time, some students said that the $229 fee for representatives of low- and middle-income countries who are members of the Society for Conservation Biology was too high.
